newsitem.title: DUBAI: Two million Moslem pilgrims mark haj in Saudi.
newsitem.headline: Two million Moslem pilgrims mark haj in Saudi.

text.p: Two million Moslems performing this year's haj pilgrimage started their journey on foot and aboard buses at dawn on Tuesday to the vast plain of Mena in Saudi Arabia, marking the start of the centuries-old rite.
Pilgrims from around 100 countries began leaving Islam's holy city of Mecca after dawn prayers at the Grand Mosque where they circled Kaaba seven times, the first haj ritual.

Saudi television showed pilgrims -- packed shoulder to shoulder in the wide marble corridors of the mosque -- struggling to touch Kaaba, a black cube-shaped building covered by gold-embroidered black silk, which Moslems across the world face to pray.

The pilgrims -- men wrapped in two simple white sheets and women in long white or black robes and headscarves -- then started the 11 km (seven mile) journey to Mena chanting "I have answered your call, God. There is no God but you."

Many walked the distance carrying umbrellas to escape the sun while others crowded on buses and on roofs of buses slowly making their way through a wave of people to Mena, where they will spend the night in air-conditioned white tents.

Saudi officials quoted by television and newspapers said the ritual has so far been trouble free. They said there was no serious congestion as 15,000 policemen patrolled the holy areas and roads leading to them and helicopters circled overhead.
Cameras installed on main roads, bridges and tunnels monitor pilgrims' movements to ensure that haj, in the past marked by tragedy, proceeds peacefully.
Up to 270 pilgrims were killed in a stampede in 1994.
Saudi officials have urged the pilgrims to abide by security instructions, especially in usually congested areas.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion on expanding sites in Mecca.
The officials made no mention of a rally that Iran said was held on Sunday in Mecca denouncing the United States and Israel in defiance of a Saudi ban on political activity during haj.
A row between Saudi Arabia and Iran has resurfaced at every haj since 1987 when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes with Saudi security. Iran boycotted the haj for three years.
But this year Iranian officials, trying to improve ties with the kingdom and other Gulf Arab states, have been using softer tones towards Riyadh even when calling for the rallies.
Riyadh has repeatedly said it would deal harshly with pilgrims who defy its ban on political activity, but there were no indications it tried to stop the Iranian rally.
Saudi officials said temperatures in Mecca were 39 Celcius (102 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday, at least five C below last year's temperatures when sun stroke and heat exhaustion were common.

At dawn on Wednesday the pilgrims will march to Mount Arafat where Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago, marking the climax of haj -- one of the five pillars of Islam and a duty each able Moslem should perform at least once.

They will head back to Mena on the same day where they will stone three monuments representing the devil. On April 17 they head back for prayers in Mecca, marking the first day of Eid al-Adha (the Feast of Sacrifice) when Moslems around the world slaughter animals and donate them to the poor.
Saudi officials said 500,000 head of sheep and 15,000 head of cattle and camels will be sacrificed by pilgrims this year.
More than 37,000 doctors, nurses, security men, bakers, cleaners and garbage collectors have been recruited to service the pilgrims -- half of them from abroad.
